title: Matplotlib Line Styles and Colors
learningObjectives: Explain the purpose and main concepts of Matplotlib Line Styles and Colors.
Create a Matplotlib Figure and Axes suitable for the visualization task.
Apply the relevant plotting API and configure its key properties.
Inspect plotted artists or chart properties to verify the intended result.
Choose labels and visual encodings that communicate data accurately.
prerequisites: NumPy arrays and basic numeric data

understand.concept: Line properties control how a plotted series appears. linestyle selects solid, dashed, dotted or dash-dot patterns; linewidth controls thickness; color selects the line color; alpha controls transparency. These properties change presentation, not the underlying data.
understand.whyItMatters: Consistent line styling helps distinguish series without misleading readers or relying on color alone.
understand.analogy: The data determines the path; line properties determine the pen used to draw it.
understand.summary: Matplotlib Line Styles and Colors is part of the Matplotlib learning path. The examples use deterministic data and the Agg backend for automated execution.

explain.narrative: Read the concept, execute each example in sequence, inspect the printed result and compare it with the expected output. Each example creates a figure with the non-interactive Agg backend and closes it after inspection.

examples.title: Set a dashed line
examples.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
line, = ax.plot([1, 2], [2, 4], linestyle='--')
print(line.get_linestyle())
plt.close(fig)
examples.explanation: A double hyphen selects a dashed line.

examples.title: Set line width
examples.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
line, = ax.plot([1, 2], [2, 4], linewidth=2.5)
print(line.get_linewidth())
plt.close(fig)

examples.title: Set a hexadecimal color
examples.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
line, = ax.plot([1, 2], [2, 4], color='#123456')
print(line.get_color())
plt.close(fig)

examples.title: Adjust transparency
examples.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
line, = ax.plot([1, 2], [2, 4], alpha=0.5)
print(line.get_alpha())
plt.close(fig)
examples.explanation: Alpha ranges from transparent to opaque.

examples.title: Combine style and width
examples.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
line, = ax.plot([1, 2], [2, 4], linestyle=':', linewidth=3)
print(line.get_linestyle(), int(line.get_linewidth()))
plt.close(fig)
examples.explanation: A dotted line can be made thicker for emphasis.

practise.guidedTask: Create a small program demonstrating matplotlib line styles and colors. Use a deterministic dataset, configure the relevant chart properties, and print at least one check that verifies the result.
practise.independentTask: Apply the technique to a small dataset of your own. Include meaningful labels, check input lengths and explain why the chosen chart is appropriate.
hints: Start with a small deterministic dataset.
Create the Figure and Axes explicitly with plt.subplots().
Inspect the relevant artist or Axes property instead of relying on visual output alone.
Add labels and units that accurately describe the data.
Close figures after automated checks or file export.
practise.challenge: Build a reusable plotting function that validates its inputs, creates the requested chart, and returns or saves a well-labelled Figure without leaking open figures.
validationCriteria: All five examples execute under the pinned Python and Matplotlib environment and match expected output.
Examples use the intended Matplotlib API correctly.
The chart type and visual encodings match the data semantics.
Labels, legends and scales are accurate and readable where applicable.
Figures are closed after automated execution.
